$comment: here so what the button deploys is reviewable and reproducible. Railway
stores templates in its own dashboard, and this is the serialized config
it holds — readable back with the template query on its public API.
Every variable carries a default — a reference to the database service or
a generated secret — so deploying asks for nothing. Keep it that way: an
empty box on the deploy form is a step someone has to research first.
Only EXPRESSIONS survive publication: a template is regenerated from a
deployed project, and Railway keeps ${{...}} references and secret()
calls but turns a plain literal into a field the deployer must fill in.
So the database service carries no literal at all — the image's own
defaults name the user and database, and PGDATA is derived from the
volume mount. Descriptions are kept here for the reader; publication

POSTGRES_PASSWORD.description: Password for the database's postgres user

PGDATA.description: Where the cluster is initialised: a subdirectory of the volume, because the mount root is never empty

PGPASSWORD.description: Required variable for the data panel

DATABASE_URL.description: Connection string for the database; the image's default user and database are both `postgres`

POSTGRES_URL.description: The database. Everything else is derived from it: the auth server, the API layer and the schema are all set up on first boot.

CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY.description: Encrypts every stored integration credential. Copy it somewhere safe — credentials cannot be read without it. 32 random bytes, as 64 hex characters.

JWT_SECRET.description: Signs the sessions the auth server issues, and the anon and service keys derived from it

WORKFLOW_JWT_SECRET.description: Signs the short-lived tokens a browser uses to join a workflow's realtime room

CRON_SCHEDULER_SECRET.description: Authenticates the in-process scheduler when it fires a schedule

SESSION_SECRET.description: Signs the application's own session cookie
